planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained soil; this compact cultivar holds its broad yellow-and-green striped leaves best in full sun.

directions: Set out container-grown plants or spring divisions in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light shade. This mounding, more compact relative of New Zealand flax produces broad, arching, strap-like leaves boldly striped lime-yellow and green, forming a bright focal clump without the towering height of the straight species. Keep it in full sun for the strongest color contrast and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor. It tolerates coastal wind and salt spray and makes an excellent accent in mixed borders, large containers, or poolside plantings.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun for the brightest pink-and-cream leaf striping.

directions: Grow in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; part shade is tolerated but muted color. This compact, gracefully arching cultivar bears strap-shaped leaves striped hot pink, cream, and green, forming a dense fountain-like mound rather than the stiffly upright habit of straight Phormium tenax. It is somewhat less cold-tolerant than the species and benefits from a sheltered site or winter mulch at the colder edge of its range. Use it as a colorful accent in borders, raised beds, or large containers where its cascading foliage can be appreciated up close.

planting.note: Plant spring divisions in well-drained soil in full sun; bronze-purple leaf color deepens with stronger sun exposure.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; this long-grown bronze-leaved form of New Zealand flax is one of the oldest and hardiest colored selections, retaining nearly the full stature and cold tolerance of the straight species. Its broad, stiffly upright, sword-like leaves emerge deep purple-bronze and hold that color well through the growing season, especially in full sun. Use it as a bold architectural specimen or background accent; it tolerates coastal exposure, wind, and drought once established.

planting.note: Plant spring divisions in well-drained soil in full sun to maintain the sharpest cream-and-green leaf striping.

directions: Grow in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to light shade; this classic variegated form of New Zealand flax produces tall, stiffly upright sword-like leaves boldly striped cream-white and green. Nearly as vigorous and cold-tolerant as the plain-leaved species, it makes a striking large-scale architectural specimen or accent for borders and coastal landscapes. It tolerates salt spray, wind, and drought once established; divide congested clumps in spring to maintain the clean variegation.

planting.note: Plant spring divisions in well-drained soil in full sun; foliage color darkens to near-black with stronger light exposure.

directions: Grow in well-drained, average soil in full sun; this dramatic cultivar produces narrow, stiffly upright leaves in the deepest near-black purple of any widely available Phormium, making it a striking contrast plant against silver or chartreuse foliage. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than the straight species and performs best with reliable moisture during establishment followed by drought tolerance once rooted in. Use it as a dark accent in mixed borders, gravel gardens, or large containers.

planting.note: Plant spring divisions in well-drained soil in full sun; pink leaf margins color up best with cooler nights and strong light.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; this large, vigorous cultivar bears broad, upright, sword-shaped leaves with bronze-green centers edged in rosy pink and cream, coloring up most intensely in cooler weather. It reaches a substantial size comparable to the straight species and makes an excellent bold specimen or screening accent. Tolerant of coastal wind, salt spray, and drought once established; remove any plain green reversion shoots at the base to keep the variegation true.

common_name: Tom Thumb Dwarf New Zealand Flax

planting.note: Plant spring divisions in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; its small scale suits containers and tight border spaces.

directions: Grow in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light shade; this genuinely dwarf cultivar forms a tidy, arching mound of narrow bronze-green leaves at a fraction of the size of standard Phormium selections, making it well suited to containers, rock gardens, and the front of mixed borders. It is somewhat less cold-tolerant than larger-growing forms and benefits from winter protection at the cooler edge of its range. Divide congested clumps in spring and keep soil on the drier side once established.
